items.title: Veeam Patches Critical Backup & Replication Authorization Bypass Vulnerability
items.summary: Veeam released security fixes for a critical authorization bypass vulnerability in Veeam Backup & Replication that lets an attacker without login credentials bypass access checks on the CDP Coordinator Service . Tracked as CVE-2026-108142, the flaw carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.1 and affects both Windows-based deployments and the Veeam Software Appliance. The company disclosed the issue on October 27, 2026, in its security advisory KB4948 . The advisory also covers two medium-severity file-write vulnerabilities in Backup & Replication and a high-severity local privilege escalation flaw in Veeam Agent for Linux. HackerOne reported all four issues. CVE-2026-108142 affects Veeam Backup & Replication 13.1.1.18 and earlier builds in the 13.1 branch, along with 13.0.2.29 and earlier builds in the 13.0 branch. Veeam identifies version 12.x as unaffected by this issue. The flaw concerns authorization, the checks that decide which actions a caller can perform. Veeam says an unauthenticated attacker can bypass those checks on the CDP Coordinator Service. However, the advisory does not describe the attack sequence or state that the vulnerability enables remote code execution . It also does not report active exploitation. Veeam Patches Backup & Replication Vulnerability Veeam lists the first fixed releases as Backup & Replication 13.1.2, build 13.1.2.57, and Backup & Replication 13.0.3, build 13.0.3.63. Administrators should match their installed version against these build numbers rather than checking only the main product version. The update also addresses CVE-2026-108140 and CVE-2026-108141, each rated medium severity with a CVSS v4.0 score of 5.9. Both require an authenticated user with the Restore Operator role who also controls the contents of a backed-up network-attached storage (NAS) share. Under those conditions, an attacker can use relative path traversal to write attacker-controlled files to an arbitrary path on the backup server. In simple terms, the file path can escape its intended folder. Veeam lists the same affected Backup & Replication builds and fixed releases for both vulnerabilities. The separate Linux issue, CVE-2026-105477, has a high-severity score of 7.3. It allows local privilege escalation and affects only Veeam Agent for Linux installations managed by Backup & Replication. Affected releases include 13.1.1.4 and earlier 13.1 builds. The fix starts with version 13.1.2, build 13.1.2.11. Cyber Security News previously reported attackers exploiting CVE-2024-40711 in Veeam to deploy Frag ransomware , highlighting backup security risks, though this separate vulnerability does not confirm exploitation of the newly disclosed authorization bypass. The publication also reported Veeam’s October security update for version 12.3.2 , noting that different product branches may require different patches. Administrators can check their installed Backup & Replication build through Help > About in the console. Veeam’s release information page provides update guidance. The company warns that attackers may study released patches to find ways into unpatched systems, making timely installation important across affected backup servers and managed Linux agents. items.title: Chrome and Firefox updates fix serious security flaws. Install them now
items.summary: On October 27, Google issued a new Stable channel update for Chrome. Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 156.0.8078.73/.74 for Windows and Mac and 156.0.8078.73 for Linux . The update includes 52 security fixes, including four rated Critical. On the same day, Mozilla issued Security Advisory 2026-118 , which fixes 167 vulnerabilities. Firefox 159 also introduces several new features. Both updates will roll out over the coming days and weeks. How to update Chrome The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update. If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, manually updating is easy. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates. If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it. Chrome version 156.0.8078.74 is up to date You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system . How to update Firefox To update Firefox, open the browser and click the menu button at the right side of the Firefox toolbar, then go to Help and select About Firefox . The About Mozilla Firefox window will open. Firefox will automatically check for updates. If one is available, it will be downloaded. Once done, you’ll be prompted to click Relaunch . After Firefox restarts, it will be up to date. After the update, the version should be 159.0 or later Technical details These Chrome and Firefox updates address a familiar problem: browser code mishandling memory while processing web content. Both releases fix use-after-free vulnerabilities, including flaws in page layout, JavaScript processing, and SVG graphics. A use-after-free vulnerability occurs when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has been freed. That can cause crashes or, in some cases, allow an attacker to run their own code. There’s another connection between these updates: both Google and Mozilla credit OpenAI Codex Security with finding bugs fixed in these releases. AI can help security teams examine browser code for weaknesses, alongside human code reviews and automated tests that check how software handles unexpected inputs. Mozilla’s collaboration with Anthropic shows how AI-discovered findings can lead to fixes: researchers validated vulnerabilities before reporting them, giving Mozilla’s team reproducible bugs to investigate, repair, and deliver to users. items.title: Hackers Compromise Camera Management Software to Deploy Malware on Windows Computers
items.summary: Hackers have compromised camera management software to deploy malware on Windows computers, using a legitimate Microsoft program to run malicious code and maintain access. The activity shows how software used to manage surveillance systems can become an entry point into business networks. The incidents followed a similar pattern: attackers gained access through the camera application, deployed a suspected reverse shell, and used DLL sideloading to contact an outside server. Like earlier cases involving abuse of monitoring tools , the activity highlights risks surrounding software trusted for routine operations. Researchers from Huntress identified the malware activity across several customer environments during September and October 2026. In their October 27 investigation, Harlan Carvey and Lindsey O’Donnell-Welch described a handful of incidents linked to compromised camera management software, while noting important gaps in understanding the initial break-in. Hackers Compromise Camera Management Software The affected application lacked embedded file version information, preventing researchers from confirming its full product name or developer. They also could not locate application logs, leaving the exact method used to compromise the software unresolved. The report does not identify a specific vulnerability or CVE. Investigators found strings connecting the executable to a domain associated with Korean company 3R Global. A camera management package available through another website contained matching strings. However, Huntress stressed that these overlaps did not establish the vendor’s identity or prove where affected customers obtained their software. After gaining access, attackers placed an executable inside a user’s application data directory. Its command line specified a remote address, a connection port, and authentication values. Combined with its location in a writable folder, these details led researchers to assess the program as a reverse shell. The attackers then copied Windows Parental Control Monitor into another application data folder. Huntress verified that this executable was a genuine Microsoft file, but its unusual location exposed the abuse. Similar VLC and VMware sideloading cases demonstrate why a trusted executable alone cannot establish that nearby libraries are safe. Here, the Microsoft program loaded malicious DLLs placed alongside it. The libraries resembled legitimate zlib compression components but had been modified to periodically contact a command-and-control server. This technique, called DLL sideloading, lets attackers execute their code through an otherwise legitimate application. The distinction matters because the executable itself was not the malicious payload. Its role was to load attacker-controlled libraries from the surrounding folder. Checking the Microsoft file’s identity without examining its location, loaded DLLs, parent process, and network activity would leave out the evidence that connected an apparently normal Windows component to the wider infection chain. Persistence, Detection, and Defensive Priorities Attackers maintained access by adding the relocated Microsoft executable to the user’s Run registry key. Windows would then launch it whenever that user signed in, restarting the loading chain. Every investigated incident involved communication with the same command-and-control IP address listed below. For defenders, the most useful signal is the connected sequence of events rather than any single filename. Camera software launching an unexpected executable, followed by a Microsoft component running from a writable folder and making unusual outbound connections, warrants investigation. Huntress specifically recommends examining that process chain. Organizations should inventory camera management applications, restrict access, and monitor their network activity. Earlier EggStreme DLL sideloading attacks also abused a Windows executable from an application data folder, reinforcing the value of checking execution locations. Where practical, Huntress recommends application controls that block unapproved executables and DLLs in user-writable directories. The investigation also leaves limits on what organizations can conclude. Huntress did not establish how the initial camera software compromise occurred, and the available evidence does not justify describing this as a confirmed vendor supply-chain breach. The immediate lesson is narrower: camera management applications need the same endpoint oversight as other business software, rather than being overlooked entirely. items.title: Pluralistic: Agents vs ecommerce (28 Oct 2026)
items.summary: Today's links Agents vs ecommerce : Opacity is a feature, not a bug. Hey look at this : Delights to delectate. Object permanence : Aibo hacking; Calculator watches; What hath Occupy wrought; Dr Seuss v Trek parody; "Blacks for Trump" x murder-cults; "9 Times My Work Has Been Ripped Off." Upcoming appearances : Vienna, Kilkenny, Courtenay, Vancouver, Folkestone, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances : Where I've been. Latest books : You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books : Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon : All the rest. Agents vs ecommerce ( permalink ) The first widely read piece of tech criticism I ever wrote was "Metacrap: Putting the torch to the seven strawmen of the meta-utopia," a response to the underlying philosophy of the "Semantic Web" that I published in 2001: https://people.well.com/user/doctorow/metacrap.htm The piece holds up surprisingly well today (if I do say so myself), and not just for its criticism of the ontological incoherence of "web semantics." The most relevant concept I develop in that piece is a criticism of any plan that starts with "first, everyone else in the world just needs to set aside their needs and advantages in favor of my priorities, and then my plan will work." This is especially relevant today in the context of "agentic AI." When this idea was first mooted, the big idea was that you could instruct a chatbot to venture out onto the public, unstructured web and it would do your bidding, for example, finding all the flights that fit your criteria and comparing prices for all of them, picking the best one and booking it for you. This idea quickly foundered. Each step in that process was too complex and specialized for a single chatbot; so the notion quickly gave way to "swarms" of specialized chatbots – one to search the web and identify likely travel websites; one to search those websites; one to evaluate flights against your criteria, one to handle the transaction, and so on. Through specialization, these bots could be made far more accurate, but at a price: both the literal price of all the extra computation that goes into powering a "swarm" versus a single process, and the reliability price that arises from complexity. That's because error rates are multiplicative: combine two bots with low failure rates into a single system and that system will have a higher failure rate than any of its components. This compounding error rate only increases as you add more and more bots, so every time you add a new specialized bot to decrease the error rate in its area of specialization, you increase the overall error rate of the system by adding more complexity to it. Despite this, companies pressed on ahead with "agentic," without any regard to the realities or consequences. For example, Microsoft has repeatedly announced that it will modify Windows to eliminate all forms of PC-side privacy and confidentiality, sending a continuous stream of screenshots to Microsoft's cloud servers so that your Microsoft "agent" can access your private data on Microsoft's cloud: https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/06/1000x-liability/#graceful-failure-modes But the real fix for "agentic" is for everyone in the world to rearrange their affairs to the benefit of AI agents. This is the same demand that the Semantic Web people made in the early oughts, and it has the same problems. The Semantic Web people operated on the assumption that there were freestanding, objectively correct ways of describing things and that everyone who put information on the web would eventually come to see that adopting these correct semantics was to everyone's advantage. In reality, these semantic differences are the expression of real, serious, unresolvable philosophical, technical, moral and political arguments. The reason that some media outlets won't describe transwomen as women isn't because they lack an appreciation of objectively correct semantic classifications – it's because they're bigots. That's the same reason "race realists" insist that there is a biological category called "race," that exists despite everything computational genomics has proved: https://pluralistic.net/2020/08/16/combat-wheelchairs/#race-realism In my book The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI , I predicted that a similar dynamic would play out when it came to agentic AI and websites. The reason websites are so inhospitable to bots is that ecommerce sites don't want to be legible to automated tools : https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374621568/thereversecentaursguidetolifeafterai/ Ecommerce websites deploy a wide range of sleazy tactics to raise prices, including surveillance pricing: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/07/gouged/#aeropain They use market power to rig whole categories, forcing prices up: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/15/enshittipedia/ Multiple law-enforcers, Republic and Democrat, state and federal, have sued companies for "drip pricing" and "junk fees" that make it impossible to know what the actual price is until you've spent a long-ass time going through the purchase process: https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/07/drip-drip-drip/#drip-off Surveillance pricing, drip pricing, junk fees, price fixing and "most favored nation" deals are the source of all the growth in profitability by the economy's largest, most important firms. These tactics require opacity and are antithetical to the kinds of automated comparison-shopping that agentic peddlers promise: https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities These tactics are facially illegal and despite this, they are widely practiced. Agents vs ecommerce (permalink)

The first widely read piece of tech criticism I ever wrote was "Metacrap: Putting the torch to the seven strawmen of the meta-utopia," a response to the underlying philosophy of the "Semantic Web" that I published in 2001:

https://people.well.com/user/doctorow/metacrap.htm

The piece holds up surprisingly well today (if I do say so myself), and not just for its criticism of the ontological incoherence of "web semantics." The most relevant concept I develop in that piece is a criticism of any plan that starts with "first, everyone else in the world just needs to set aside their needs and advantages in favor of my priorities, and then my plan will work."

This is especially relevant today in the context of "agentic AI." When this idea was first mooted, the big idea was that you could instruct a chatbot to venture out onto the public, unstructured web and it would do your bidding, for example, finding all the flights that fit your criteria and comparing prices for all of them, picking the best one and booking it for you.

This idea quickly foundered. Each step in that process was too complex and specialized for a single chatbot; so the notion quickly gave way to "swarms" of specialized chatbots – one to search the web and identify likely travel websites; one to search those websites; one to evaluate flights against your criteria, one to handle the transaction, and so on.

Through specialization, these bots could be made far more accurate, but at a price: both the literal price of all the extra computation that goes into powering a "swarm" versus a single process, and the reliability price that arises from complexity. That's because error rates are multiplicative: combine two bots with low failure rates into a single system and that system will have a higher failure rate than any of its components. This compounding error rate only increases as you add more and more bots, so every time you add a new specialized bot to decrease the error rate in its area of specialization, you increase the overall error rate of the system by adding more complexity to it.

Despite this, companies pressed on ahead with "agentic," without any regard to the realities or consequences. For example, Microsoft has repeatedly announced that it will modify Windows to eliminate all forms of PC-side privacy and confidentiality, sending a continuous stream of screenshots to Microsoft's cloud servers so that your Microsoft "agent" can access your private data on Microsoft's cloud:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/06/1000x-liability/#graceful-failure-modes

But the real fix for "agentic" is for everyone in the world to rearrange their affairs to the benefit of AI agents. This is the same demand that the Semantic Web people made in the early oughts, and it has the same problems. The Semantic Web people operated on the assumption that there were freestanding, objectively correct ways of describing things and that everyone who put information on the web would eventually come to see that adopting these correct semantics was to everyone's advantage.

In reality, these semantic differences are the expression of real, serious, unresolvable philosophical, technical, moral and political arguments. The reason that some media outlets won't describe transwomen as women isn't because they lack an appreciation of objectively correct semantic classifications – it's because they're bigots. That's the same reason "race realists" insist that there is a biological category called "race," that exists despite everything computational genomics has proved:

https://pluralistic.net/2020/08/16/combat-wheelchairs/#race-realism

In my book The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI, I predicted that a similar dynamic would play out when it came to agentic AI and websites. The reason websites are so inhospitable to bots is that ecommerce sites don't want to be legible to automated tools:

https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374621568/thereversecentaursguidetolifeafterai/

Ecommerce websites deploy a wide range of sleazy tactics to raise prices, including surveillance pricing:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/07/gouged/#aeropain

They use market power to rig whole categories, forcing prices up:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/15/enshittipedia/

Multiple law-enforcers, Republic and Democrat, state and federal, have sued companies for "drip pricing" and "junk fees" that make it impossible to know what the actual price is until you've spent a long-ass time going through the purchase process:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/07/drip-drip-drip/#drip-off

Surveillance pricing, drip pricing, junk fees, price fixing and "most favored nation" deals are the source of all the growth in profitability by the economy's largest, most important firms. These tactics require opacity and are antithetical to the kinds of automated comparison-shopping that agentic peddlers promise:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities

These tactics are facially illegal and despite this, they are widely practiced. Cheating is so profitable that it's cheaper for firms to buy off regulators and pay fines than it is for them to stop criming. The fantasy that these same companies would welcome agentic shopping bots with open arms is just as implausible as the idea that if we feed enough words to the word-guessing program, it will wake up and become a "super intelligence":

https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/18/surprise/#wow-signal

What's more, the AI companies know this. Google's big plan to make AI profitable is to sell merchants the power to combine its surveillance data with its AI tools to price-gouge shoppers:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/21/cod-marxism/#wannamaker-slain

And right on time, ecommerce websites are mass-blocking AI agents:

https://gizmodo.com/online-shopping-platforms-turn-against-third-party-ai-agents-2000831298

They're doing it in part because AI agents allow shoppers to cheat (for example, by renewing a "temporary" hold on a used item to block other buyers indefinitely), but also because they don't want automation tools on their platforms at all. These tools are a frontal assault on all the most exciting (and sleaziest) ways to make money in the waning hours of end-stage capitalism. Far from welcoming bots, ecommerce sites were always going to block them.

It's easy to come up with amazing applications for technology if you're allowed to assume that you can get everyone else in the world to set aside their priorities and their interests in favor of yours. But unless someone has a plan to do that, we shouldn't take them seriously.

items.summary: Hackers have begun testing a critical Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that can let them run commands without logging in. Threat intelligence firm Defused reported exploratory exploit attempts against its decoy systems on October 27, 2026. However, these observations do not confirm successful attacks against customer systems, and Oracle had already released a patch before the activity was detected. Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the flaw carries a critical CVSS score of 9.8. Horizon3.ai discovered the issue and reported it to Oracle on July 24. Oracle fixed it on October 20 through its October Critical Patch Update . Although initially reported privately as a zero-day, it was a publicly disclosed, patched vulnerability when Defused observed the probes. Oracle EBS 0-Day Vulnerability The weakness affects the Core component of Oracle Application Object Library in EBS versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. It requires network access over HTTP or HTTPS but needs neither valid credentials nor user interaction. Cyber Security News previously covered the issue in its report on Oracle’s October security update . According to Horizon3.ai’s technical advisory , the vulnerable Thin Client Framework servlet is reachable at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer . A crafted request can trigger SQL injection, allowing an attacker to send database commands as the powerful APPS database user. That access can then be chained into operating system command execution under the EBS application account. The impact extends beyond database access. Successful exploitation could expose or alter financial, payroll, human resources, and purchasing records accessible to APPS. However, these observations do not confirm successful attacks against customer systems, and Oracle had already released a patch before the activity was detected.

Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the flaw carries a critical CVSS score of 9.8. Horizon3.ai discovered the issue and reported it to Oracle on July 24. Oracle fixed it on October 20 through its October Critical Patch Update. Although initially reported privately as a zero-day, it was a publicly disclosed, patched vulnerability when Defused observed the probes.

Oracle EBS 0-Day Vulnerability

The weakness affects the Core component of Oracle Application Object Library in EBS versions 12.2.3 through 12.2.15. It requires network access over HTTP or HTTPS but needs neither valid credentials nor user interaction. Cyber Security News previously covered the issue in its report on Oracle’s October security update.

According to Horizon3.ai’s technical advisory, the vulnerable Thin Client Framework servlet is reachable at /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer. A crafted request can trigger SQL injection, allowing an attacker to send database commands as the powerful APPS database user. That access can then be chained into operating system command execution under the EBS application account.

items.title: FortiBleed 2.0 Reveals Thousands of Fortinet VPN and Active Directory Credentials in Exposed Configurations
items.summary: FortiBleed 2.0 investigation, published October 27, revealed 40,573 cleartext secret records in exposed FortiGate configurations, including 37,076 local-user passwords and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records linking firewall access, VPN services, and internal identity systems. The researchers examined 1,703 configuration-report files containing 101,419 credential and account records associated with 1,689 host identifiers. The material also includes administrator logins, email-server passwords, and high-availability cluster secrets. These figures reflect records, not unique users, confirmed physical devices, or credentials that still work today. Despite its name, FortiBleed 2.0 is a follow-up investigation based on recently obtained files, not a newly disclosed vulnerability. Most files are dated February 20, 2026, while 31 are undated, leaving the timing of initial access and configuration theft unconfirmed. FortiBleed 2.0 Exposes Fortinet VPN and AD Credentials Compared with the first dataset, researchers identified 924 additional host identifiers and 975 domain labels absent from the earlier collection. Overview of Hudson Rock’s free FortiBleed lookup portal However, domain labels can belong to service providers, registration contacts, or account holders. They should not be read as 975 newly compromised companies. The findings expand earlier FortiBleed credential exposure coverage by revealing accounts and services behind perimeter logins. The associated toolchain extracts firewall configurations, recovers stored secrets, and attempts further access. Its parsing workflow collects local users, administrator entries, LDAP connections, cluster settings, and email credentials. Some stored FortiOS ENC values can be recovered offline when configurations use the system-default encryption key. Recovery depends on the software version, settings, and available material. Cavalier Exposes 54 Credential Records Across Two Hosts Exposed local-user passwords may support VPN access, but account status, access rules, reachability, and multifactor authentication determine whether login succeeds. Hudson Rock’s analysis identified 7,437 disabled local-user records containing cleartext data. Empty MFA fields do not necessarily indicate missing MFA, as external authentication systems may enforce it. LDAP bind credentials deserve close attention because they connect FortiGate appliances to directory services. An account with excessive rights could increase the impact of a breach. Ordinary LDAP query access, however, does not automatically grant domain-administrator privileges. Earlier reporting on FortiGate configuration theft highlights this route toward internal access. Cavalier’s Breach Data Fortinet’s response guidance calls for terminating administrator and VPN sessions, resetting credentials, enforcing MFA, updating firmware, and restricting management access. Security teams should compare current settings with a trusted configuration and examine firewall and domain-controller logs for unexpected activity. The configuration findings also call for reviewing LDAP bind passwords, cluster secrets, and email-server credentials. Investigators should verify ownership of recurring administrator accounts such as fgtsecure and forticloud-sync before treating them as unauthorized. Account names alone do not establish malicious activity. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Your security tool flagged the sensitive file. Can anyone still read it?
items.summary: Part 1 split AI agents into two kinds and looked at the controls BigID and Varonis are building for them. Part 2 covered what protecting the data does for each kind, and where it stops. This part is about how to tell, during an evaluation, which kind of tool you’re actually looking at. DLP, DSPM, and data-centric protection do different jobs A lot of tools get called data security, and buyers often assume they overlap more than they do. Data loss prevention (DLP) watches the ways data leaves your company, like email, web uploads, and USB drives, and blocks or flags what looks sensitive. Data security posture management (DSPM) scans where data is stored, classifies it, and flags exposure, such as a folder anyone in the company can open. Both find data and watch what happens to it, and that’s valuable. Data-centric protection acts on the data once it’s found. It encrypts, masks, redacts, quarantines, or deletes it, so the file is protected without waiting on someone to respond to an alert. One doesn’t replace the other. Going by their own published materials, neither BigID nor Varonis encrypts data natively. BigID orchestrates encryption through separate tools, and Varonis’s core platform discovers, classifies, and monitors without native encryption. Both do a good job of showing where sensitive data lives and who or what touched it, and both do things PK Protect doesn’t, including DLP and governing agent access. Neither is designed to make a file unreadable to an agent that reached it without permission. Five questions to ask in any DSPM or DLP evaluation 1 When the tool flags that someone or something reached a sensitive file it shouldn’t have, what happens to the file? If the answer is that an alert fires, ask what that person or agent can do with the contents before someone acts on the alert. 2 Is encryption built into the platform, or does it come from a separate tool? A separate tool is one more thing to buy, deploy, and keep in sync, and any gap between discovery and protection leaves classified data unprotected. 3 Does the protection stay with the file when the file moves? Files get copied and exported to places nobody planned for, and they’re only protected there if the protection is part of the file. 4 Does it cover mainframe and on-prem systems, or only cloud and SaaS? Many DSPM tools started in the cloud. If your sensitive data is on z/OS, IBM i, or file servers in your own data center, ask about those specifically. 5 How does it handle each kind of AI agent as their numbers grow? For assistants working on a person’s behalf, ask how it helps you cut down what each person can reach, since the assistant can reach the same things. For agents with their own identity, ask whether each new one has to be found and given permissions before it’s covered, or whether the data stays unreadable to it either way. Why the first question matters A readable file in the wrong hands is expensive. IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report put the average U.S. breach at $10.22 million. The number of identities that could reach that file is growing too. Machine identities now outnumber human ones about 109 to 1, and 40% of them can reach company data. A DSPM or DLP tool can flag a file and still leave it readable to whatever copies it. Changing that takes something that protects the data itself. Where PK Protect fits PK Protect is built for that part of the problem. It finds sensitive data on endpoints, in the cloud, in Microsoft 365, and on z/OS and IBM i, and classifies it under one classification policy. From there, your team can encrypt, mask, redact, quarantine, or delete what it finds. Protection stays on the file after it moves, so an agent running under its own identity can’t read an encrypted file without access to the key. For assistants working on a person’s behalf, cleaning up overexposed data and masking or redacting values people don’t need limits what those assistants can surface. Format-preserving encryption keeps protected data usable for the systems that depend on it. To be clear about the limits, PK Protect won’t stop a file transfer while it’s happening, it won’t tell you what your agents are doing, and it won’t stop an assistant from reading what its user is allowed to read. If you’d like to see what sensitive data is in your environment today and what it would take to protect it, request an assessment . items.title: Waiting on a Node.js Upgrade? Build a Stopgap with the Controls You Own
items.summary: Executive Summary Node.js has fixed CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, but upgrading at scale is slow. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of roughly 3 million Node.js installations have been patched, and 1.7 million run end-of-life lines that will never receive a fix. In the meantime, interim mitigations from the Qualys Threat Research Unit narrow the Brotli, DNS, TLS, and keep-alive attack paths, and WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major vendors add further layers. Soon, Qualys ETM will factor these controls into risk scores. These controls buy time, but upgrading the runtime remains the only complete fix. Node.js comes with a clear instruction: upgrade the runtime. The October 21 security release fixes 10 vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, and three high-severity flaws that weaken DNS and TLS hostname validation. Fixed releases exist for the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines. Upgrading at this scale still takes time, because the vulnerable code lives in the runtime itself, in container images, single-executable applications, and serverless functions that dependency checks never touch. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of the 3.3 million installations have been patched so far, and 1.7 million run end-of-life versions, including 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, and 20.x, that will not receive a fix and must move to a supported line. Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while upgrades roll out, and the right visibility shows which runtimes need attention first. Our Node.js blog post covers vulnerabilities, fixed versions, and detection methods. Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and upgrade, in four steps: find and prioritize exposed Node.js, apply interim mitigations, layer the controls you already run, then patch and verify. Step 1: Find and Prioritize Exposed Node.js Qualys customers can search for assets affected by CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to see every Node.js runtime across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads. That includes copies that dependency checks miss, such as those in version managers, application folders, and bundled runtimes. It is important to note that not every vulnerable runtime has the same level of exposure. Start with internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data (CVE-2026-111497), since they are the most direct path to remote code execution. Services that open TLS connections to user-supplied hosts (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483) come next. Runtimes on end-of-life lines need an upgrade plan, as no patches will be available for them. Consider these factors alongside business criticality to decide what to mitigate and upgrade first. Step 2: Apply Interim Mitigations Node.js has no official workaround, but the Qualys Threat Research Unit has identified practical interim steps. Each one narrows a specific attack path while you plan the upgrade, and together they complement the fix. These changes do not eliminate all exploitation paths associated with these CVEs, and some changes may affect application behavior. Therefore, it is crucial to test the affected applications after each change. Limit Brotli exposure (CVE-2026-111497). Avoid decompressing Brotli from untrusted sources where you can, and cap payload size and decompression ratio at the reverse proxy or WAF. Use the safer DNS call (CVE-2026-105482). Resolve user-supplied names with dns.lookup instead of dns.resolve* , and reject hostnames that contain NUL characters. Canonicalize IP addresses (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483, CVE-2026-106072). Convert addresses to canonical form before they reach a TLS connection, and reject fullwidth and other non-canonical forms. Turn off keep-alive for untrusted servers (CVE-2026-105481). Disable keepAlive on http.Agent for connections to servers you do not control. Treat the Permission Model as advisory. (CVE-2026-106071, CVE-2026-106073) Do not rely on it as a security boundary on affected versions. Step 3: Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run The tools already in your environment can work alongside the interim steps, each at a different point in the attack path. Each layer can catch what the one before it misses. Edge and network: WAF and IPS. WAF and IPS vendors such as Cloudflare, Fortinet, and Check Point have released protections that name the Brotli flaw. They help block exploit requests before those requests reach the Node.js decoder. After exploitation: EDR. Behavioral and exploit-prevention policies in endpoint tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Cortex XDR add a second line of defense. They help stop what an attacker tries next, such as a Node.js process spawning a shell or downloading a binary, and some also act on the memory exploitation itself. Node.js 3rd-party Mitigation and Compensating Controls The table below lists the rules and policies each vendor has released for CVE-2026-111497 and the related Node.js CVEs, ready to copy into your console. Layer Vendor Control CVEs How it helps Edge (WAF) Cloudflare Managed rule 8f252673b6 9d47afb21f8 8acca706f3c, Brotli – Request Content-Encoding CVE-2026-111497 Matches inbound requests that declare Content-Encoding: br. It ships in Log mode, so set it to Block. Network (IPS) FortiGate IPS signature 62703 CVE-2026-111497 Blocks the crafted request inline before it reaches the decoder. Network (IPS) Check Point Advisory CPAI-2026-15802 CVE-2026-111497 Blocks the exploit attempt at the gateway. Host (EDR) CrowdStrike Suspicious Process Prevention (Linux, macOS, Windows) CVE-2026-111497, 106070, 106071, 106073 Blocks a Node.js process that spawns shells, downloaders, or newly written binaries after exploitation. Host (EDR) CrowdStrike ASLR Bypass Prevention (Windows) CVE-2026-111497 Blocks the ASLR bypass a reliable Brotli exploit needs. Requires Additional User Mode Data. Host (EDR) Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Behavior Monitoring (Windows, Linux, macOS) CVE-2026-111497, 106070, 106071, 106073 Inspects process ancestry and autostart changes to catch follow-on activity after exploitation. Host (EDR) Cybereason Exploit Protection Mode (Windows) CVE-2026-111497 Applies per-process memory-exploit mitigations. Host (EDR) SentinelOne Anti Exploitation / Fileless (Windows) CVE-2026-111497 Behavioral AI that detects in-memory exploitation inside the Node.js process. Host (EDR) Cortex XDR Known Vulnerable Processes Protection (Linux, macOS, Windows) CVE-2026-111497 Injects exploit-prevention logic into the Node.js process. Effective only if Node.js is in the protected process set. Host (EDR) Cortex XDR Credential Gathering Protection (Linux, macOS) CVE-2026-106071, 106073 Blocks unauthorized reads of credential stores, such as SSH keys and password files, that a Permission Model bypass could reach. Coverage is strongest for the Brotli flaw. The Cloudflare rule keys on the Content-Encoding header, so it covers requests that declare Brotli, not compressed data a service fetches or unpacks from other sources. The DNS and TLS hostname flaws depend on the interim steps above and on the upgrade. Note: Rule and policy IDs are as published by each vendor in October 2026; confirm them in your console. The endpoint policies act after exploitation or on memory behavior, so verify each one fires for your Node.js process. Compensating controls reduce risk; upgrading Node.js remains the only complete fix. Step 4: Patch, Restart, and Re-Validate Interim mitigations reduce risk. Upgrading remains the only complete fix. Node.js fixed these flaws in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, while lines such as 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, 20.x, and older receive no fix and must move to a supported release. Customers can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate, so check the patch catalog for their line. Qualys reports a high patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for the runtime upgrade. Confirm That Remediation Is Complete A patch isn’t finished when the package installs: Upgrade every copy. Migrate end-of-life lines to a supported release. Rebuild container images and single-executable applications on the fixed version, then redeploy them. Restart every service that runs on Node.js. Long-running processes, containers, and single-executable applications keep the vulnerable runtime in memory until they restart. Rescan and verify. Rescan with Cloud Agent or Container Security and confirm the detection QIDs are closed. Where to Start Find. Search for CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to locate every runtime, including copies outside standard install paths. Prioritize. Put internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data at the top, alongside business criticality. Mitigate. Apply the Qualys TRU interim steps to runtimes awaiting an upgrade, and test the affected applications. Layer. Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers, and set the Cloudflare rule to Block. Patch and verify. Upgrade to a fixed release, rebuild and redeploy what embeds the runtime, restart every Node.js service, and rescan. Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched. Coming Next: Give Your Controls Credit in Qualys ETM The capabilities described in this section are in development and subject to change. Two servers can run the same unpatched Node.js build and carry very different risks. One sits behind a WAF rule and an IPS signature that name the Brotli flaw, with EDR watching its Node.js process. The other faces the internet with nothing in front of it. A traditional scan reports them the same way. Qualys ETM is being extended to close that gap. It arrives in three steps: Recommendations on every finding (coming soon). ETM will show which applicable third-party controls can reduce exposure for each vulnerability, so teams know what to enable and where. Controls reflected in the score. Controls that are in place will lower a finding’s QVSS score to reflect your actual defenses, shown as the Environmental score, so remediation queues focus on what still needs attention. Action from the same platform. Teams will be able to apply third-party mitigations through TruRisk Eliminate from the platform that found the exposure. Download the Node.js exposure dashboard today. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of the 3.3 million installations have been patched so far, and 1.7 million run end-of-life versions, including 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, and 20.x, that will not receive a fix and must move to a supported line.

Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while upgrades roll out, and the right visibility shows which runtimes need attention first. Our Node.js blog post covers vulnerabilities, fixed versions, and detection methods.

Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and upgrade, in four steps: find and prioritize exposed Node.js, apply interim mitigations, layer the controls you already run, then patch and verify.

Step 1: Find and Prioritize Exposed Node.js

Qualys customers can search for assets affected by CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to see every Node.js runtime across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads. That includes copies that dependency checks miss, such as those in version managers, application folders, and bundled runtimes.

It is important to note that not every vulnerable runtime has the same level of exposure. Start with internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data (CVE-2026-111497), since they are the most direct path to remote code execution. Services that open TLS connections to user-supplied hosts (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483) come next. Runtimes on end-of-life lines need an upgrade plan, as no patches will be available for them. Consider these factors alongside business criticality to decide what to mitigate and upgrade first.

Step 2: Apply Interim Mitigations

Node.js has no official workaround, but the Qualys Threat Research Unit has identified practical interim steps. Each one narrows a specific attack path while you plan the upgrade, and together they complement the fix.

These changes do not eliminate all exploitation paths associated with these CVEs, and some changes may affect application behavior. Therefore, it is crucial to test the affected applications after each change.

  • Limit Brotli exposure (CVE-2026-111497). Avoid decompressing Brotli from untrusted sources where you can, and cap payload size and decompression ratio at the reverse proxy or WAF.
  • Use the safer DNS call (CVE-2026-105482). Resolve user-supplied names with dns.lookup instead of dns.resolve*, and reject hostnames that contain NUL characters.
  • Canonicalize IP addresses (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483, CVE-2026-106072). Convert addresses to canonical form before they reach a TLS connection, and reject fullwidth and other non-canonical forms.
  • Turn off keep-alive for untrusted servers (CVE-2026-105481). Disable keepAlive on http.Agent for connections to servers you do not control.
  • Treat the Permission Model as advisory. (CVE-2026-106071, CVE-2026-106073) Do not rely on it as a security boundary on affected versions.
Step 3: Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run

The tools already in your environment can work alongside the interim steps, each at a different point in the attack path. Each layer can catch what the one before it misses.

Edge and network: WAF and IPS. WAF and IPS vendors such as Cloudflare, Fortinet, and Check Point have released protections that name the Brotli flaw. They help block exploit requests before those requests reach the Node.js decoder.

After exploitation: EDR. Behavioral and exploit-prevention policies in endpoint tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Cortex XDR add a second line of defense. They help stop what an attacker tries next, such as a Node.js process spawning a shell or downloading a binary, and some also act on the memory exploitation itself.

Node.js 3rd-party Mitigation and Compensating Controls

The table below lists the rules and policies each vendor has released for CVE-2026-111497 and the related Node.js CVEs, ready to copy into your console.

Coverage is strongest for the Brotli flaw. The Cloudflare rule keys on the Content-Encoding header, so it covers requests that declare Brotli, not compressed data a service fetches or unpacks from other sources. The DNS and TLS hostname flaws depend on the interim steps above and on the upgrade.

Note: Rule and policy IDs are as published by each vendor in October 2026; confirm them in your console. The endpoint policies act after exploitation or on memory behavior, so verify each one fires for your Node.js process. Compensating controls reduce risk; upgrading Node.js remains the only complete fix.

Step 4: Patch, Restart, and Re-Validate

Interim mitigations reduce risk. Upgrading remains the only complete fix. Node.js fixed these flaws in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, while lines such as 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, 20.x, and older receive no fix and must move to a supported release. Customers can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate, so check the patch catalog for their line. Qualys reports a high patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for the runtime upgrade.

Confirm That Remediation Is Complete

A patch isn’t finished when the package installs:

  1. Upgrade every copy. Migrate end-of-life lines to a supported release.
  2. Rebuild container images and single-executable applications on the fixed version, then redeploy them.
  3. Restart every service that runs on Node.js. Long-running processes, containers, and single-executable applications keep the vulnerable runtime in memory until they restart.
  4. Rescan and verify. Rescan with Cloud Agent or Container Security and confirm the detection QIDs are closed.
Where to Start
  1. Find. Search for CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to locate every runtime, including copies outside standard install paths.
  2. Prioritize. Put internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data at the top, alongside business criticality. 
  3. Mitigate. Apply the Qualys TRU interim steps to runtimes awaiting an upgrade, and test the affected applications.
  4. Layer. Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers, and set the Cloudflare rule to Block.
  5. Patch and verify. Upgrade to a fixed release, rebuild and redeploy what embeds the runtime, restart every Node.js service, and rescan. 

Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched.

Coming Next: Give Your Controls Credit in Qualys ETM

The capabilities described in this section are in development and subject to change.

Two servers can run the same unpatched Node.js build and carry very different risks. One sits behind a WAF rule and an IPS signature that name the Brotli flaw, with EDR watching its Node.js process. The other faces the internet with nothing in front of it. A traditional scan reports them the same way.

Qualys ETM is being extended to close that gap. It arrives in three steps:

  1. Recommendations on every finding (coming soon). ETM will show which applicable third-party controls can reduce exposure for each vulnerability, so teams know what to enable and where.
  2. Controls reflected in the score. Controls that are in place will lower a finding’s QVSS score to reflect your actual defenses, shown as the Environmental score, so remediation queues focus on what still needs attention.
  3. Action from the same platform. Teams will be able to apply third-party mitigations through TruRisk Eliminate from the platform that found the exposure.

items.title: From Hijacked PBX to Stolen Trunk: INJ3CTOR3’s Campaign Evolves
items.summary: Executive Summary In May, Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs (CRIL) documented JOMANGY , a PHP webshell generation deployed by INJ3CTOR3 with self-healing persistence channels and a built-in toll-fraud dialer. Back then, the fraud ran through the victim's own PBX, so removing the implant would have stopped it. Artifacts we collected from the operator's C2 staging servers during mid-September 2026 show that this is no longer true: the installer now sends credentials off the box on every run, and a second staging host serves it. INJ3CTOR3's FreePBX implant now uploads the victim's SIP trunk, AMI, database, and mail-relay credentials to the operator, so disinfecting or rebuilding an infected host no longer ends the exposure. Anyone running FreePBX, Issabel, or Elastix who suspects compromise must rotate the secrets in 17 configuration files, and only after the host is clean. The infection and persistence code is nearly unchanged; what the operator rotated are the identifiers that were available to defenders since the last time. Each section below pairs a finding with what to do about it. Key Takeaways Credentials leave on every run. k.php uploads 17 configuration files to both staging hosts every minute the host stays infected. The fraud no longer needs your PBX. A stolen trunk secret lets the operator register and place calls as you from anywhere. Last report's identifiers have expired. Each build now carries its own watermark, and the webshell gate hash was rotated. Two staging hosts. Plain-text commands now point to 160[.]119[.]69[.]4, while base64-encoded ones still use 45[.]95[.]147[.]178. Clean-looking logs and consoles prove nothing. Requests through an encoded space reach the shell without being named in the access log, and trunks are written directly to /etc/asterisk; they do not appear in the FreePBX console. The Campaign So Far INJ3CTOR3 has been abusing Asterisk-based phone systems for toll fraud since at least 2020. Check Point Research named the operation that November, when it exploited CVE-2019-19006 in FreePBX and used a basic webshell to read amportal.conf and sip_additional.conf by hand. Unit 42 reported a related operation against Elastix in 2022, Fortinet documented the EncystPHP webshell in January 2026, and our May report covered JOMANGY. The playbook has held for six years: scan for exposed PBXs, exploit or brute-force a way in, plant a password -gated webshell, and dial out at the victim's expense. Figure 1 below shows the chain as it stands in the September build, now including the credential upload back to the staging hosts. Figure 1: INJ3CTOR3 attack chain, September generation. (Source: 0x1da5 GitHub) What Changed Since Our Last Report We compared the April artifacts behind our May report with the 9 September collection from both staging hosts, after decoding every layer. Area April September Credential Exfiltration None 17 files to /hima_data/index.php on both hosts Staging hosts 45[.]95[.]147[.]178 45[.]95[.]147[.]178 and 160[.]119[.]69[.]4 webshell watermark One value in every copy A different value per build Webshell gate hash (JOMANGY and ZenharR) a2f6863413c4192a4abfa360577b9961 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a /x takeover script 367 lines 620 lines, mostly added cleanup: removing rival actors’ implants and SSH keys wor.php, people2.txt, _*.php status files Present Absent from the collection Unchanged: the decoded webshell panel, the encoding chain (base64 in the shell script, base64 again in PHP, then ROT13), the persistence channels, the backdoor account password hash, and the borrowed timestamp. Behavioral detections built on our May report still apply. Credential Exfiltration: The Implant Is No Longer the Product The September k.php ends with two new base64-encoded lines, each holding 17 curl commands that upload one configuration file apiece to /hima_data/index.php, one line per staging host (See Figure 2 below). The paths are typed out by hand and cover FreePBX, Issabel, and Elastix layouts. The collector path echoes hima, a backdoor account the takeover script creates. The name goes back further: Check Point's 2020 INJ3CTOR3 report shows a Telegram post by a user called Hima sharing a tool that scans and cracks SIP ranges, saving its output as HimaResults. Figure 2: k.php line 34, decoded into 17 file uploads Three of the cron beacons fetch and run k.php every minute (the others every two or three minutes), so the upload repeats every minute during the infection. Rotating credentials on a still-infected host hands the new secrets to the operator within minutes. What it unlocks Files uploaded Rotate SIP trunks and extensions (chan_sip) /etc/asterisk/sip.conf, sip_additional.conf, sip_registrations.conf, sip_general_additional.conf, sip_custom.conf Every trunk secret (with your carrier) and extension secret, changed in the FreePBX GUI, since the *_additional.conf files are regenerated SIP trunks and extensions (PJSIP) /etc/asterisk/pjsip.auth.conf, pjsip.endpoint.conf, pjsip.aor.conf, pjsip.identify.conf, pjsip.transports.conf The same secrets; review IP-based identity rules Call origination without SIP /etc/asterisk/manager.conf Every AMI user. PBX database, AMI, and platform admin /etc/freepbx.conf, /etc/amportal.conf, /etc/asterisk/amportal.conf, /etc/issabel.conf, /etc/elastix.conf The database password (AMPDBPASS), the MySQL root password, and any AMI password stored there Outbound mail /etc/postfix/sasl_passwd The SMTP relay account, with your mail provider This opens a second route to fraud. Our May report covered calls placed through the webshell, which require the shell to be alive and to land in the victim's own call records. With a stolen trunk secret, the operator can register to the carrier from any machine and call as the victim, leaving nothing on the host, unless the carrier also restricts the trunk to the victim's IP addresses. A successful disinfection stops the first route; only rotation stops the second. Detection Network: outbound HTTP POSTs from a PBX to any /hima_data/ path or to either staging host. A PBX seldom needs outbound web access beyond vendor updates, so egress allow-listing closes this channel. Carrier: alert on trunk registrations from outside your own IP ranges, and on premium or international destinations, off-hours calling, and unusual concurrency. Set spend caps and destination blocks where your carrier offers them. For Law Enforcement Agencies and CERTs By design, victims' credentials were collected on the two staging hosts, which stopped responding in late September 2026. Going offline does not end exposure: hosting providers may still retain server data, and infected PBXs keep trying to upload their credentials every minute to addresses that could be reassigned to someone else. Both are reasons for law enforcement and national CERTs, which have the legal standing that researchers lack, to work with the providers on preserving that data and sinkholing the addresses, which would also identify victims for notification. We saw the uploads in code; we did not capture one in transit and hold no victim list. Two Staging Hosts, Split by Encoding An infected host now talks to both staging hosts, and which one depends on whether the command was written in plain text or base64. The /x takeover script is byte-identical on both. Reference Encoding Points to k.php line 2 (re-runs /x), eight cron schedules in /x, wr.php's callback Plain text 160[.]119[.]69[.]4 Camouflaged cron payloads, login-triggered stager Base64 45[.]95[.]147[.]178 Credential upload Base64 Both In April, all of these pointed to 45[.]95[.]147[.]178. We assess that the operator replaced the address in plain text and never re-encoded the base64 strings; the credential upload, which names both hosts, appears deliberate. This host is distinct from the scanner 160[.]119[.]76[.]250, which is named in our May report. Defend: block both hosts in both directions, and decode every base64-encoded string in a crontab or shell profile before deciding which hosts a host talks to. A plain-text review would miss every channel that still reaches 45[.]95[.]147[.]178. The Webshell: Same Program, New Identifiers Decoded, the September JOMANGY panel is identical to April's except for the values defenders were told to look for. Per-build watermark. Our May report advised hunting for trace_e1ebf9066a951be519a24140711839ea, present in every April copy. The September builds carry trace_bd42a8a0d23ae16c85dede7d2abaec05 (45[.]95[.]147[.]178) and trace_7544725ebaaadac217dfaa7ca8e8fe7e (160[.]119[.]69[.]4), so that hunt now misses current infections. One gate for two generations. JOMANGY and ZenharR share a single hardcoded MD5 gate hash, rotated together from a2f6863413c4192a4abfa360577b9961 to 8b3a1d970fda0c17a0b785a990fb7b6a. Our May report listed the April value under ZenharR only. A forged administrator session. Behind the gate, the FreePBX button builds an admin session using FreePBX's own ampuser class and setAdmin(); in our lab, it opened the full console without any password. Therefore, changing the FreePBX admin password affects neither the gate nor this session. (See Figure 3 below) Figure 3: The panel's Freepbx and Elastix buttons forge an admin session without a password Because each of these identifiers changes between builds, the detection approach later in this report focuses on who put a file on disk rather than on what the file contains. The .htaccess Door and the Access-Log Gap k.php writes a seven-line .htaccess to /var/www/html/admin/views/. It does not hide the webshell; it unblocks it, and it lets requests reach a copy without naming it. RewriteEngine On # enable symbolic links Options +FollowSymLinks RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-d RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-f RewriteCond %{REQUEST_FILENAME} !-l RewriteRule ^\s+ config.php [L] Request path Status What answered /dir/zzz 404 Nothing /dir/%20zzz, /dir/%09zzz (space, tab, etc) 200 config.php /dir/+zzz 404 Nothing Simulating an operator and a victim in an isolated environment, we confirmed that a request to a URL containing an encoded space returned a working webshell for the attacker. The access log records only the requested path, never the file that answered, so searching logs for the webshell by its filename can return nothing on a host that is serving it . Defend: check every .htaccess across the web root for who put it there; one that no package, FreePBX module, or member of your team accounts for is suspect, whatever it contains. Because the takeover script wipes logs, treat log hunting as secondary: requests with %20, %09, or %0A directly after a slash that return 200 are worth a look where logs survive. What the FreePBX Console Won't Show You FreePBX lists the trunks it created from its own database; Asterisk reads whatever is in its configuration files. In our lab, a trunk we wrote directly into /etc/asterisk/pjsip_custom.conf carried a call while the FreePBX Trunks page reported no records (See Figure 4 below). We did not see the campaign plant one, but its root-equivalent accounts and stolen trunk secrets give the operator everything needed to do so. Figure 4: Our lab trunk, known to Asterisk and carrying calls, invisible in the FreePBX console Defend: audit from the Asterisk CLI (pjsip show endpoints, pjsip show registrations, sip show peers, sip show registry) and compare with what the console lists. Review the *_custom.conf files for trunks or contexts that nobody on your team added. What Keeps It There Before detecting or cleaning, it helps to see the whole apparatus. Everything in Figure 5 is read from /x and k.php: ways the implant stays on the box, and doors allowing the operator to come back, through a system account or a single web request. Each piece can rebuild/repair all others under a minute, which is why removing any one of them on its own fails. (See Figure 5 below) Figure 5: Persistence channels that rebuild each other, and the backdoors they stay open Detecting It Without IOCs The operator rotates hashes, watermarks, gate values, and hosts between builds, so asking whether a file is known-bad quickly stops working. The better question is who put the file there: compare what is on disk with what the package manager or a clean install says it should be. On the host: triage with beagle.sh PBX admins can run beagle.sh , a report-only script that makes no changes to the host, to check a PBX server for signs of compromise. (See Figure 6 below) Check What it flags Packed shells Several identical, same-size PHP files across unrelated directories Locked files chattr +i or +a under the web root or in hidden directories Unowned .htaccess An .htaccess no installed package accounts for Self-rebuilding cron A cron line that downloads a file and hands it to a shell Accounts An extra UID-0 account, or a full-permission FreePBX admin, nobody created Blocklist Addresses dropped in and out by iptables outside fail2ban's chains Figure 6: beagle.sh (Source: 0x1da5 GitHub ) The script separated one infected server from one clean server of the same FreePBX version, a sample of one, so expect some legitimate findings. However, it cannot tell you whether the credentials have already been left: that happens during the first cron run, within a minute of infection, and long before anyone scans. The upload leaves no file behind, and the takeover script wipes what might have recorded it: the web server, Asterisk, cron and audit logs, plus shell and MySQL histories, which makes forensic timelines hard to reconstruct. With telemetry The most distinctive actions leave little on disk; in our detonation, backdoor accounts were created and deleted 27 seconds apart. These eleven behaviors are detection strategies to build into your own tooling: Layer Behavior What it catches Host crond spawns a shell that downloads a file and runs it The takeover script on its single run, before persistence and before credentials leave Host The web server account spawns a shell The webshell's command box in use Host A cron child rewrites the crontab every minute without reading it first Beacon reinstallation Host chattr +i or touch -r on a file in the web root The lock and the borrowed timestamp Host Twelve PHP files were written to the web root in the same second The webshell copies, as they are written; fan-out Network The PBX contacts staging host roughly every 60 seconds The beacon's rhythm, whatever the address Network Many configuration files read, then outbound POST requests Credentials leaving Web A request with leading encoded whitespace returns 200 for a path not on disk The .htaccess door Decoy Any read of a decoy config file that the implant reads, but nothing legitimate does Credential collection, with no false positives by design Phone Channels originate over AMI or the CLI outside your dial plan A call asking for nothing legitimate Phone CDRs with premium destinations, off-hours calling and unusual concurrency The fraud itself The last two catch the fraud rather than the machinery, whatever the files are called, and whether you ever find the shell. The host rows need process telemetry that PBX appliances rarely have, which is part of why so many stay infected. Why Cleanup Fails, and the Order That Works First move Why it fails on its own Delete the webshell Cron re-runs k.php within minutes and rewrites all 12 copies, the .htaccess, and the immutable flags. Patch FreePBX Sangoma's advisory for CVE-2025-57819 states the fix prevents new exploitation but does not clean a compromised system. Change the admin password The gate and the forged session never use it, and the backdoor accounts bypass the FreePBX login. Shadowserver data showed more than 900 compromised FreePBX instances in February 2026; over 700 of them were still compromised in May. Rebuilding from a clean image is the most reliable fix; if you clean in place, work from the system layer up, because it replants everything above it. Preserve first The takeover script truncates logs, then deletes them, and clears shell and database history, so evidence shrinks with every run: Cut the host off from the internet, or at least block all outbound traffic except to your SIP carrier. Blocking only the two known staging hosts is not enough if the operator has moved. With no route out, the minute-by-minute downloads fail, and nothing more is uploaded. One local loop survives: a watchdog cron line re-runs the cached copy of k.php at /var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2 every minute, rebuilding the webshells offline, which is why cron comes first in the cleanup below. Capture all crontabs and the eight backups listed below, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, shell profiles, and the web root with lsattr output and change times. Export the FreePBX ampusers table, the call records database, and the Asterisk full log, and ask your carrier to preserve CDRs and registration logs. Then clean, in this order Cron and its spares. Clear root's crontab in one go, so the restore and watchdog lines are removed. Then kill any running zen2, devnull2, or serv processes; killed earlier, the watchdog restarts them within a minute. Remove the k.php beacons (/var/lib/asterisk/bin/zen2, devnull2, zen222, devnull312, devnull212, /tmp/.cache/update, /dev/shm/.systemd/kernel). Unlock (chattr -i, -a) and delete the eight crontab backups: /usr/lib/.systemd/.cache, /usr/share/.fonts/.config, /var/lib/.dbus/.data, /var/tmp/.X11/.Xauthority, /opt/.local/.bashrc, /var/cache/.fontconfig/.cfg, /etc/.ssl/.cert, and /root/.config/.pref. Login and boot triggers. Remove the base64 stager from /root/.bash_profile, /root/.bashrc, and /etc/rc.local. Accounts and SSH. Remove every extra UID-0 account and any account whose /etc/shadow hash begins with $1$nRz1Cbtk$ (legitimate service accounts with that hash need new passwords, not deletion). Restore sshd_config, where root login was re-enabled. Web application. Remove the 12 webshell copies, the .htaccess, the freepbxusers row in ampusers, and /var/www/html/admin/modules/freepbx_ha/license.php. Credentials. Only now rotate the secrets in the 17 files and across every account on the host. Conclusion The hard part of the campaign used to be getting the implant off the box, and that has not changed. What has changed is that the box is no longer the whole problem: an organization that rebuilds but does not rotate has removed the operator's calling platform and handed over its carrier account. The code ties this generation to the actor in our May report through the takeover script, backdoor hash, and staging host, and a gate rotated in step across JOMANGY and ZenharR. The operator is now rotating exactly the strings defenders were given, so detections built on provenance and behavior will outlast this build, and detections built on its hashes will not. CRIL continues to monitor INJ3CTOR3's infrastructure. Indicators of Compromise Hashes and strings rotate between builds; use them to confirm a finding, not as your only detection.
